blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 13 (Halogens), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the atomic and physical properties of the common halogens (fluorine to iodine): electron structure, physical state, colour, and the trend in melting and boiling points. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Halogens are the Group 17 (VIIA) elements; they are very reactive non-metals and exist as diatomic molecules X₂ in all phases.

Electron structure: every halogen has seven electrons in its outer shell (ns²np⁵): F 2, 7 (2s²2p⁵); Cl 2, 8, 7 (3s²3p⁵); Br 2, 8, 18, 7 (4s²4p⁵); I 2, 8, 18, 18, 7 (5s²5p⁵).

Physical state and colour at room temperature: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a greenish yellow gas, bromine a volatile reddish-brown liquid with corrosive and toxic fumes, and iodine a shiny greyish black solid that sublimes to a violet vapour. The colours darken from chlorine to iodine because of changes in the absorption of light by electron transitions within the molecules.

Melting and boiling points rise down the group (Table 13.1), because the molecules become larger and the London forces stronger:

book_ref.quote: Table 13.1 Atomic and Physical properties of the common halogens.

blocks.prompt: 2 What is volatility? Explain how London dispersion forces decide the volatility and the physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine. Summarise the effect of molecular size in a table. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Volatility is the ease with which a substance evaporates; it is inversely related to the boiling point, so a more volatile substance has a lower boiling point.

Forces: halogen molecules are non-polar, so the forces between them are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id, London dispersion) forces. They depend on molecular size, shape and polarizability. Stronger forces need more energy to separate the molecules from the liquid to the gaseous phase, giving higher boiling points and lower volatility.

Trend: down the group the molecular mass and the size of the outer shell increase and the London forces become stronger, so volatility decreases from chlorine to iodine.
• Chlorine: small molecules, weak id-id forces; a gas at room temperature, the most volatile, disperses quickly in air.
• Bromine: bigger molecules with stronger forces; a liquid, less volatile than chlorine but more than iodine; it evaporates readily giving toxic fumes.
• Iodine: the strongest forces in the group; a solid, the least volatile.

Effect of size (Table 13.2):

book_ref.quote: Larger, more polarizable molecules with stronger London dispersion forces have higher boiling points and lower volatility.

blocks.prompt: 3 Discuss the bond strength of the halogen molecules with the help of Table 13.3. Why is fluorine an exception to the trend? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bond energies (Table 13.3): F₂ 156, Cl₂ 243, Br₂ 193, I₂ 151 kJ mol⁻¹.

General trend: from chlorine to iodine the bond energy decreases gradually. The atomic size increases down the group, so the bond length becomes longer and the bond weaker: Cl₂ (243) > Br₂ (193) > I₂ (151).

Fluorine as an exception: by size alone F-F should be the strongest bond, but it is only 156 kJ mol⁻¹, weaker than Cl-Cl and Br-Br. Fluorine atoms are very small, so in the F₂ molecule the lone pairs on the two atoms (three on each atom, Fig. 13.1) are very close together. The significant electron-electron repulsion between these lone pairs weakens the bond despite the high electronegativity of fluorine.

Overall order: Cl₂ > Br₂ > F₂ > I₂.

book_ref.quote: Due to the small size, there is significant electron–electron repulsion between the lone pairs on the fluorine atoms

blocks.prompt: 4 What happens when each halogen is added to aqueous solutions of the other halide ions? Write balanced ionic equations for the displacements that occur and explain the results using the E° values of Table 13.4. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Halogens act as oxidizing agents: they gain electrons and become halide ions. A halogen oxidizes and displaces the halide ions of the halogens below it.

Fluorine displaces all the other halide ions:
F₂(g) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + Cl₂
F₂(g) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + Br₂
F₂(g) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + I₂

Chlorine displaces Br⁻ and I⁻:
Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

Bromine displaces only I⁻: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂

Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion, so it gives no reaction.

Explanation: E° (X₂/X⁻) becomes less positive from fluorine to iodine, showing decreasing oxidizing power. A halogen with a higher E° oxidizes the halide ion of a halogen with a lower E°. Oxidizing power: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

book_ref.quote: Fluorine molecule can oxidize and displace all the halide ions from their solutions

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the reactions of fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine with hydrogen, giving the conditions and equations, and name the acid each hydrogen halide forms in water. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids. Reactivity with hydrogen decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

Fluorine: reacts explosively even at low temperature and in the dark.
H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g); in water HF forms hydrofluoric acid.

Chlorine: reacts readily in the presence of UV light or a spark, giving colourless HCl gas.
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) (hν); in water it forms hydrochloric acid.

Bromine: reacts with hydrogen upon heating; the reaction is exothermic.
H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g) (heat); HBr forms strong hydrobromic acid in water.

Iodine: reacts only at high temperature in the presence of a catalyst; the reaction is reversible and very slow.
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) (catalyst); HI forms hydroiodic acid in water.

book_ref.quote: When halogen elements react with hydrogen, they produce hydrogen halides.

blocks.prompt: 6 Compare the trend in the bond energies of the halogen molecules X₂ (Table 13.3) with that of the hydrogen halides H-X (Table 13.5). Explain why fluorine is out of order in X₂ but not in H-X, and state the order of thermal stability of HX. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Values: X₂: F₂ 156, Cl₂ 243, Br₂ 193, I₂ 151 kJ mol⁻¹. H-X: H-F 569, H-Cl 431, H-Br 366, H-I 299 kJ mol⁻¹.

X₂ trend: bond energy decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ because larger atoms give longer, weaker bonds. F₂ is an exception: the very small fluorine atoms bring their lone pairs close, and the strong lone-pair repulsion weakens the F-F bond.

H-X trend: bond dissociation energy falls regularly from H-F to H-I, with fluorine at the top. Fluorine's high electronegativity and small atomic radius give strong orbital overlap with hydrogen and a very strong H-F bond. Down the group the larger halogen atom gives reduced overlap: H-Cl is weaker than H-F, H-Br weaker still, and the very large iodine atom gives poor overlap and the weakest bond, H-I.

Thermal stability follows the H-X bond strength: HF > HCl > HBr > HI. HF is the most thermally stable and HI the least.

book_ref.quote: Bond strength between the hydrogen and the halogen atom in the H-X molecule explain this trend.

blocks.prompt: 7 Using Table 13.5, calculate the energy needed to break all the H-X bonds in 10.0 g of HF and in 10.0 g of HI (H = 1, F = 19; take I from Table 13.1). How many times greater is the first value, and what does this show about thermal stability? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find moles from mass and molar mass, then multiply by the bond dissociation energy per mole.

book_ref.quote: The bond dissociation energy of H-F (569 kJ/mol) is the highest among the hydrogen halides.

steps: Molar masses: HF = 1 + 19 = 20 g mol⁻¹; HI = 1 + 126.9 = 127.9 g mol⁻¹.
Energy for HF = 0.500 × 569 = 284.5 kJ; energy for HI = 0.0782 × 299 = 23.4 kJ.
Ratio = 284.5/23.4 ≈ 12.2. HF needs far more energy (strong H-F bond, 569 kJ mol⁻¹), so HF is the most and HI (299 kJ mol⁻¹) the least thermally stable.
blocks.final_answer: HF: 284.5 kJ; HI: 23.4 kJ; about 12 times; HF is far more thermally stable than HI.

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain, ion by ion, how electronegativity, ionic size and charge density decide the strength of fluoride, chloride, bromide and iodide ions as reducing agents. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A halide ion acts as a reducing agent by giving up its extra electron. Down the group electronegativity decreases and the ionic radius increases; this lowers the charge density and makes electron donation easier. Order of reducing power: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.

Fluoride (F⁻): fluorine is highly electronegative and holds its extra electron by a strong bond. The small F⁻ ion has a high charge density, which stabilizes it, so it hardly loses an electron; F⁻ is the weakest reducing agent.

Chloride (Cl⁻): larger in size and chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine, so Cl⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than F⁻ but weaker than Br⁻ and I⁻.

Bromide (Br⁻): bromine is less electronegative than chlorine; Br⁻ has a larger ionic radius and lower charge density, so it loses an electron easily and is stronger than Cl⁻.

Iodide (I⁻): iodine has much lower electronegativity and I⁻ is large, with low charge density, so it donates an electron most readily; I⁻ is the strongest reducing agent among the halides.

book_ref.quote: This trend is mostly due to the decreasing electronegativity and increasing atomic radius down the group.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe how aqueous silver nitrate followed by aqueous ammonia is used to identify fluoride, chloride, bromide and iodide ions. Give the equations and observations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Step 1, aqueous AgNO₃: halide ions react with Ag⁺ to form insoluble silver halides: X⁻(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) → AgX(s). This is the silver nitrate test used in qualitative analysis.
• F⁻: no visible reaction, because silver fluoride is soluble in water.
• Cl⁻: white precipitate, Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
• Br⁻: cream-coloured precipitate, Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s).
• I⁻: yellow precipitate, Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s).

Step 2, aqueous ammonia tests the solubility of the precipitates:
• AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia forming the colourless diamminesilver(I) complex: AgCl(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
• AgBr dissolves only in concentrated ammonia: AgBr(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq).
• AgI does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia.
• For F⁻ there is no precipitate, so ammonia has no effect.

Summary (Table 13.6):

book_ref.quote: provides a systematic way to differentiate between halide ions

blocks.prompt: 10 A solution containing 1.17 g of sodium chloride is treated with excess aqueous silver nitrate. Calculate the mass of silver chloride precipitated, and the mass of ammonia needed to dissolve this precipitate completely in dilute aqueous ammonia (Na = 23, Ag = 108, N = 14, H = 1; Cl from Table 13.1). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: One Cl⁻ gives one AgCl, and each AgCl takes two NH₃ to form [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.

book_ref.quote: Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia to form diamminesilver(1) complex.

steps: NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g mol⁻¹; moles NaCl = 1.17/58.5 = 0.0200 mol = moles AgCl.
blocks.final_answer: AgCl precipitated = 2.87 g; ammonia needed = 0.68 g.

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the reactions of solid sodium fluoride, chloride, bromide and iodide with concentrated sulfuric acid. Give equations and observations and relate the differences to the reducing power of the halide ions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
NaF: fumes of hydrogen fluoride are produced. NaF(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HF(g). HF is a weak reducing agent, so it does not react with H₂SO₄ further.

NaCl: fumes of hydrogen chloride are produced. NaCl(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HCl(g). No further reaction.

NaBr: steamy fumes of HBr, brown fumes of bromine and the smell of SO₂. It is a redox reaction:
NaBr + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HBr(g)
2HBr(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → Br₂(g) + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
HBr reduces sulfuric acid to SO₂ (S: +6 → +4) and is itself oxidized to bromine.

NaI: fumes of HI, purple fumes of iodine and the smell of H₂S:
NaI + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HI(g)
8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l)
HI is a strong reducing agent; it reduces H₂SO₄ to H₂S (S: +6 → -2) and is itself oxidized to I₂.

Relation: the reducing power of the halide ions increases from fluoride to iodide, so the reactions become more complex: F⁻ and Cl⁻ give only HX, Br⁻ reduces the acid to SO₂, and I⁻ reduces it further to H₂S.

book_ref.quote: The nature of the product and nature of reaction changes down the group from fluoride to iodide.

blocks.prompt: 12 16.18 g of hydrogen bromide reacts completely with concentrated sulfuric acid according to the balanced equation 2HBr(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → Br₂(g) + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Calculate the masses of bromine and sulfur dioxide formed (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16; Br from Table 13.1), and show the change in oxidation state of sulfur. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Two moles of HBr give one mole of Br₂ and one mole of SO₂.

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen bromide acts as a reducing agent by reducing sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide and is self-oxidized to bromine.

steps: Sulfur: +6 in H₂SO₄ → +4 in SO₂ (reduced by 2); bromine: -1 in HBr → 0 in Br₂ (two Br atoms each lose one electron).
blocks.final_answer: Br₂ = 15.98 g; SO₂ = 6.40 g; sulfur is reduced from +6 to +4.

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain why the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide is a disproportionation reaction, and balance its equation by matching the electrons lost and gained by chlorine. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Disproportionation: a reaction in which a single element undergoes both oxidation and reduction simultaneously.

Products with hot NaOH: sodium chloride (NaCl) and sodium chlorate(V) (NaClO₃). Oxidation states of chlorine: Cl₂ = 0, NaCl = -1, NaClO₃ = +5. Some chlorine is reduced (0 → -1) and some is oxidized (0 → +5) in the same reaction, so it is a disproportionation.

Balancing by electrons:
• Each Cl reduced to Cl⁻ gains 1 electron.
• Each Cl oxidized to ClO₃⁻ loses 5 electrons.
• For the electrons to balance, 5 Cl atoms must be reduced for every 1 Cl atom oxidized: 6 Cl atoms = 3Cl₂.
• This gives 5NaCl and 1NaClO₃; sodium needs 6NaOH, and hydrogen and oxygen balance with 3H₂O.

3Cl₂(g) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)
Check: Cl 6 = 5 + 1; Na 6 = 5 + 1; O 6 = 3 + 3; H 6 = 6.

With cold NaOH the oxidized product is NaClO (chlorine +1) instead: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. So the temperature decides the products.

blocks.prompt: 14 35.5 g of chlorine gas is passed into excess cold aqueous sodium hydroxide. Calculate the masses of NaOH used and of NaCl, NaClO and water formed, and show that mass is conserved (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1; Cl from Table 13.1). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O: one mole Cl₂ needs two moles NaOH and gives one mole of each product.

book_ref.quote: Chlorine undergoes disproportion when it reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide

steps: Cl₂ = 71.0 g mol⁻¹; moles Cl₂ = 35.5/71.0 = 0.500 mol.
NaOH used = 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 40.0 g.
Reactants: 35.5 + 40.0 = 75.5 g; products: 29.25 + 37.25 + 9.0 = 75.5 g, so mass is conserved.
blocks.final_answer: NaOH 40.0 g; NaCl 29.25 g; NaClO 37.25 g; H₂O 9.0 g (total 75.5 g on both sides).

blocks.prompt: 15 42.6 g of chlorine reacts completely with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide according to the balanced equation 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O. Calculate the masses of NaOH used and of NaCl and NaClO₃ formed (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1; Cl from Table 13.1). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use the mole ratio Cl₂ : NaOH : NaCl : NaClO₃ = 3 : 6 : 5 : 1.

book_ref.quote: Chlorine is oxidized from 0 to +5 in NaClO₃.

blocks.final_answer: NaOH used 48.0 g; NaCl 58.5 g; NaClO₃ 21.3 g.

blocks.prompt: 16 How do the active species formed from chlorine in water destroy micro-organisms? Explain why HOCl is more effective than OCl⁻. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Formation of the active species: chlorine hydrolyses in water, Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq). Chloric(I) acid (hypochlorous acid, HOCl) is a weak acid and partially dissociates: HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻ (chlorate(I) or hypochlorite ion). HOCl and OCl⁻ are the primary active species.

Action on micro-organisms (both are oxidizing agents):
• They oxidize essential cell components such as proteins and lipids, disrupting cell function and leading to cell death.
• They oxidize and inactivate enzymes that are crucial for the survival and replication of bacteria.
• They oxidize nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), preventing bacteria from replicating and from vital cellular functions.

Why HOCl is more effective: HOCl has a neutral charge, which allows it to penetrate the cell walls of micro-organisms easily; the charged OCl⁻ ion is less effective.

book_ref.quote: Essential cellular components such as proteins and lipids are oxidized by HOCl and OCl⁻

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the factors that affect the disinfection of water by chlorine. Why is swimming-pool water given slightly more chlorine? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. pH: at pH around 6-7.5, HOCl predominates and disinfection is more effective. At higher pH (above 7.5), OCl⁻ predominates; it is less effective but still provides disinfection. (HOCl is more effective because its neutral charge lets it penetrate cell walls.)

2. Chlorine dose: the higher the amount of chlorine, the more effective the disinfection. Sufficient chlorine must be added to produce enough HOCl and OCl⁻ to kill the bacteria.

3. Contact time: the contact time of water with chlorine must be long enough to allow the disinfectants to penetrate and kill bacteria, viruses and protozoa.

Swimming pools: the water is likely to contain a higher concentration of bacteria, so it is chlorinated with slightly higher concentrations of chlorine. In small quantities chlorine is harmless to humans but poisonous to the disease-causing bacteria, and chlorination is a relatively inexpensive method of disinfection.

book_ref.quote: At pH around 6-7.5, HOCl predominates and makes the disinfection process more effective.
